question.note: Whether the substance use and friendship association from heterogeneous schools holds in AI-majority schools (Q2; quote p.2 is Q2's span), role of substance use (Q3).
Generic: which structural and individual-level factors shape the networks. Names no structural pattern (Q4 partial) and no specific attribute (Q1 partial).

central_claim.note: The abstract's 'rather than risky behaviors' wording, credited per the gold decision.

evidence.note: Original network survey data, 9th/10th grade, three Northern Plains reservation schools (E1, as in the calibration; cross-sectional not stated). N = 247 as in the abstract (E2 partial); ERGMs (E3 partial).
Structural terms and actor attributes in the models (E3 part); measured domains listed without the measures (E5 partial, as the calibration did for a domain list).

key_findings.note: 'Strong and consistent' is the paper's wording.

Exceptions not named. 'In any of the three schools' is slightly strong given the alcohol homophily exception in School B (p<0.01), but the paper's own p.16 says substance use 'is not associated with relational patterns', so not flagged (cf. B1; not a catch).
Gender and grade only; no sexual orientation.
Incoming-tie centralization only in School C (half of F5). 'Potentially reflecting egalitarian norms' keeps the paper's hedge ('may reflect', p.15); not flagged.

scope_and_limits.note: One time point for 9th/10th graders; life course and school transitions.

Peer-perception imputation may be biased; the possible inflation of similarity among friends is not stated. 'Sensitivity analyses confirmed the null findings held' fits 'reverse no substantive conclusion' (p.7).

theoretical_positioning.note: SNA/ERGM and adolescent peer network literature (vague T1); challenging generalizability from heterogeneous settings is half of T3.

interlocutor_claim.note: Receiver effects and homophily, disputed for AI-majority schools. Moody et al. 2011 (ref 6), Ali et al. 2014 (ref 13) and Schaefer et al. appear in Table 1 for these effects.

flags.text: The note says the link was used as a basis for 'effective' network-based prevention interventions; the paper says intervention research built on it had 'promising results' (p.16).
